name: Jeremiah
author: Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, from a family of priests in Anathoth, a small village a few miles north of Jerusalem. He was called as a prophet, someone who spoke God's messages to the people, while still young, and kept speaking for about forty years, often at great personal cost. His call is traditionally dated to around 627 BC, though some scholars think that date marks his birth and that his public work began nearer 609 BC. His friend and scribe Baruch wrote down many of his words. Traditionally Jeremiah is seen as the book's source; many scholars think his followers later collected and arranged it, noting that the ancient Greek version is shorter and ordered differently.
audience: Jeremiah spoke first to the kings, priests and ordinary people of Judah and its capital, Jerusalem, a small kingdom caught between powerful empires. Many of them refused to listen, and some tried to silence him. Later parts address those deported to Babylon and the refugees who fled to Egypt after Jerusalem fell.
era: Jeremiah lived through the collapse of the Assyrian Empire and the rise of Babylon. Good King Josiah led a sweeping religious reform around 622 BC but was killed in battle by Egypt's Pharaoh Necho in 609 BC. After Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC, Judah became its subject, and repeated rebellions led to a first deportation of Jerusalem's leaders in 597 BC. In 587 or 586 BC the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem and its temple and carried many more into exile.

notes.1:1: Anathoth was a village of priests in the tribe of Benjamin's land; Jeremiah's call is dated to Josiah's thirteenth year, around 627 BC.
notes.3:6: This message is dated to King Josiah's reign, when the northern kingdom of Israel had already been conquered by Assyria about a century earlier.
notes.7:1: This 'temple sermon' is widely linked with chapter 26, early in Jehoiakim's reign around 609 BC; Shiloh, where the tabernacle (the portable worship tent) once stood, had long since been destroyed.
notes.11:18: The plotters were men from Jeremiah's own hometown of Anathoth, possibly including members of his priestly family.
notes.13:1: The place named 'Perath' is usually taken as the distant Euphrates River, though some think it means Parah, a spring near Anathoth.
notes.14:1: The heading links this passage to a severe drought in Judah; its exact date is not known.
notes.19:1: The Valley of Ben Hinnom, just south of Jerusalem, contained Topheth, a site where children had been sacrificed to foreign gods.
notes.21:1: Set around 588 BC, when King Zedekiah sent messengers to Jeremiah as Nebuchadnezzar's Babylonian army besieged Jerusalem.
notes.22:10: Shallum is another name for King Jehoahaz, Josiah's son, who reigned three months in 609 BC before Pharaoh Necho took him captive to Egypt.
notes.22:13: Aimed at King Jehoiakim, who reigned 609–598 BC and was known for building himself a lavish palace using forced, unpaid labour.
notes.22:24: Coniah is King Jehoiachin, who reigned only three months before being taken to Babylon in 597 BC.
notes.24:1: Set just after 597 BC, when King Jehoiachin, Judah's officials and skilled craftsmen had been deported to Babylon.
notes.25:1: Dated to Jehoiakim's fourth year, 605 BC, the year Nebuchadnezzar became king and Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish.
notes.26:1: Dated to the start of Jehoiakim's reign, around 609 BC; the elders recall Micah, who prophesied about a century earlier under King Hezekiah.
notes.27:1: Around 594 BC, envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon met in Jerusalem, apparently to plan rebellion against Babylon.
notes.28:1: Dated to Zedekiah's fourth year, around 593 BC, when hopes ran high that the exiles of 597 BC would soon return.
notes.29:1: A letter Jeremiah sent to the exiles in Babylon, carried by royal envoys, a few years after the deportation of 597 BC.
notes.30:1: Chapters 30–33 are often called the 'Book of Consolation'; some think parts were first addressed to descendants of the long-conquered northern kingdom.
notes.31:15: Ramah, a town north of Jerusalem, was later where captives were gathered before deportation; one old tradition placed Rachel's tomb in Benjamin's territory, not far from Ramah, though the better-known site is near Bethlehem.
notes.32:1: Dated to Zedekiah's tenth year, around 587 BC, during the final siege, while Jeremiah was confined in the palace guardhouse.
notes.34:1: During the final siege, Lachish and Azekah were the last fortified towns in Judah still holding out besides Jerusalem.
notes.34:8: During the siege, owners freed their Hebrew slaves, then took them back when the Babylonian army briefly withdrew to face Egypt.
notes.35:1: The Rekabites were a clan who lived in tents and avoided wine; under Jehoiakim they took refuge in Jerusalem from invading armies.
notes.36:1: Dated to Jehoiakim's fourth year, 605 BC; the public reading followed in his fifth year, during a fast, in late 604 BC.
notes.37:1: Set around 588 BC, when an Egyptian army marched north and the Babylonians temporarily lifted their siege of Jerusalem.
notes.39:1: Jerusalem's walls were breached in the summer of 587 or 586 BC, after a siege of about eighteen months.
notes.40:7: Gedaliah, from a respected family of officials, was appointed governor by Babylon and ruled from Mizpah, a town north of Jerusalem.
notes.43:8: Tahpanhes was an Egyptian border fortress in the eastern Nile Delta, where the Jewish refugees, taking Jeremiah with them, settled.
notes.44:1: Addressed to Jewish communities scattered across Egypt, from Migdol and Tahpanhes in the north to Memphis and Pathros, meaning Upper Egypt.
notes.45:1: Dated to 605 BC, when Baruch was writing down Jeremiah's words on the scroll described in chapter 36.
notes.46:1: Chapters 46–51 contain messages about foreign nations; this one recalls Egypt's defeat by Babylon at Carchemish, on the Euphrates, in 605 BC.
notes.46:13: Concerns Nebuchadnezzar's expected invasion of Egypt; Babylonian records mention a campaign against Egypt around 568 BC.
notes.47:1: Addressed to the Philistines on the coast west of Judah, dated before an attack by Pharaoh on their city of Gaza.
notes.48:1: Moab was a kingdom east of the Dead Sea, a long-time neighbour and frequent rival of Israel and Judah.
notes.49:1: Ammon lay east of the Jordan River, around Rabbah, the site of modern Amman in Jordan.
notes.49:7: Edom lay south-east of the Dead Sea; Teman and Bozrah were among its chief places.
notes.49:23: Damascus was the capital of Aram, Israel's northern neighbour, with Hamath and Arpad farther north in Syria.
notes.49:28: Kedar was an Arab tribe of the desert east of Judah, known for tents and herding. Hazor here is not the famous northern city but probably refers to Arab settlements in the same region.
notes.49:34: Elam was a kingdom east of Babylon, in what is now south-western Iran; this message is dated to early in Zedekiah's reign.
notes.50:1: Chapters 50–51 concern Babylon itself, the empire then dominating Judah; some scholars date parts to later in the exile.
notes.51:59: Dated to Zedekiah's fourth year, around 593 BC, when royal official Seraiah, Baruch's brother, travelled to Babylon with the king.
notes.52:1: This closing chapter closely matches the account in 2 Kings 24–25 and is generally thought to have been added by a later editor.
notes.52:28: These deportation figures, smaller than those in 2 Kings, may count only adult men or a particular group.
notes.52:31: Around 561 BC, the new Babylonian king Evil-merodach (Amel-Marduk) released Jehoiachin after thirty-seven years in prison.
